article.overview: A radio occultation instrument measures how a radio signal is bent, delayed and shifted in phase as it passes through a planetary atmosphere or ionosphere, typically when the transmitter or receiver is hidden behind the body being studied. On the Moon, the technique is used to probe the thin layer of electrically charged plasma around the surface, which is roughly 100 km thick [4]. The flown example examined here is the dual-frequency radio science (DFRS) experiment on India's Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [1][2]. A CubeSat-based concept, RIPLIO, has been proposed but has not been flown [4]. The payload class is defined by its measurement technique rather than by one hardware design, so no single set of specifications applies to every radio occultation instrument.
article.description: A radio occultation experiment uses a radio link between two spacecraft, or between a spacecraft and a ground station. As the link passes behind the Moon or through its plasma environment, the phase of the signal changes. Scientists convert this phase history into refractivity and, within an ionosphere, into electron density along the ray path [4][5]. The Chandrayaan-2 orbiter transmits coherent S-band (2240 MHz) and X-band (8496 MHz) signals to a ground station at Byalalu, near Bangalore [1][2]. The DFRS team describes the two frequencies as a way to reduce the influence of Earth's own atmosphere on the measurement [1]. Twelve occultation experiments were conducted in campaign mode on four occasions [1]. The sources reviewed describe the DFRS as a radio-science experiment that uses the orbiter's coherent signals; they do not give a hardware breakdown of the orbiter or ground equipment.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a lunar radio occultation instrument is to determine the electron content, density profile and structure of the lunar ionosphere. The lunar ionosphere is only weakly constrained by observation, and its formation mechanisms and dynamics remain unresolved [4]. The Chandrayaan-2 DFRS results report total electron content (TEC) of up to 1.5 TECU in the lunar wake region, with a stated uncertainty of 0.15 TECU, and a plasma density of about 10^4 cm^-3 in the wake, at least an order of magnitude above dayside values [1]. A three-dimensional lunar ionospheric model developed at the Space Physics Laboratory, which is a numerical model rather than a direct observation, suggests that Ar+ and Ne+ are the dominant ions in the wake region [2]. The Watson et al. study links better lunar ionosphere mapping to lunar exploration hazard assessment [4].
article.operating_principle: The basic observable in a radio occultation measurement is the phase change of the signal between transmitter and receiver. In Earth-orbit GNSS radio occultation, after the effects of satellite motion and clock drift are removed, the remaining atmospheric effect appears as a bending of the signal path, which is then related to the refractive index of the medium [5]. In an ionosphere, the refractive index depends on electron density, so the phase perturbation can be inverted to give electron content and vertical electron density profiles [4][5]. The Watson et al. concept study proposes to use VHF signals at multiple frequencies for this purpose, because the phase perturbations of VHF signals passing through the ionosphere can be analysed to infer electron content and high-resolution vertical profiles [4]. Retrievals in Earth GNSS radio occultation typically assume near spherical symmetry, and side-looking occultations are usually discarded [5]. The sources reviewed for the lunar cases do not state whether the same assumption is used.
article.scientific_importance: The Moon's ionosphere cannot be investigated adequately through a small number of observations. Its structure, dynamics and formation are poorly constrained because observations are very limited and existing results disagree significantly [4]. Chandrayaan-2 DFRS provides flown, dual-frequency measurements of the wake region, showing plasma densities at least an order of magnitude above the dayside values [1]. These measurements add to a very sparse observational record, against which the earlier Apollo-era evidence, which is model-dependent, can be compared [1][8].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a radio occultation instrument. The hardware differs between a flown orbiter radio experiment with an Earth ground station, a proposed CubeSat crosslink pair, and historical spacecraft radio links that were used for occultation-style tests. The sources reviewed do not publish mass, power or dimensions for the DFRS or RIPLIO hardware, so these values are reported as not publicly specified rather than estimated.

examples.name: Apollo-era lunar radio links
examples.type: Historical spacecraft radio links (not a dedicated occultation instrument)
examples.status: Historical. Apollo 15 command module signals were received after the spacecraft passed behind the lunar limb, as reported in a 1971 Nature letter [6]. The Apollo 15 and Apollo 16 subsatellites each carried S-band transponders [7].
examples.ionospheric_occultation_results: The sources reviewed do not report ionospheric occultation results from the subsatellites [7][8]. According to a search-result summary of the ROLSS/arXiv paper, interpretation of Apollo-era and Luna data is model-dependent: one analysis read the Luna data as consistent with no significant lunar ionosphere, while Apollo ALSEP measurements suggested a near-surface photoelectron layer [8].
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed

examples.name: RIPLIO CubeSat crosslink concept
examples.status: Proposed concept based on simulation [4][9]. No hardware is described as built or flown [4].
examples.configuration: Constellation of at least two CubeSats in lunar orbit. One satellite carries a VHF transmitter broadcasting at multiple frequencies; another carries a broadband receiver. Together they would make crosslink radio occultation measurements of the lunar ionosphere [4].
examples.simulation_result: The authors report that simulations show two CubeSats in lunar orbit would substantially increase observational capacity [4]. A 2025 CAP Congress abstract reports an updated simulation study using more realistic ionosphere models; according to a search-result summary of that abstract, lower HF signal frequencies and frequency spacings of a few MHz are most responsive to lunar plasma. The abstract emphasises refining requirements, so it is a preliminary step rather than a feasibility study [9].
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed [4]

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for the Chandrayaan-2 DFRS hardware or the RIPLIO CubeSats in the sources reviewed [1][2][4]. Apollo-era spacecraft radio hardware dimensions are not stated in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for the Chandrayaan-2 DFRS hardware or the RIPLIO CubeSats in the sources reviewed [1][2][4]. No mass value is estimated in this article.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for any example.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A radio occultation measurement requires a suitable geometry: the signal path must cross the ionosphere or wake region, and the transmitter and receiver must be positioned so that the path is refracted by the plasma. The Chandrayaan-2 experiments were performed in campaign mode rather than as continuous monitoring [1]. The flown configuration uses the Byalalu ground station as its Earth-side receiver [1]. The measurement depends on a stable frequency reference; the reported oscillator stability of about 10^-11 is a search-result summary and has not been verified [10]. The plasma environment is itself demanding, with ionospheric layers about 100 km thick and wake-region densities that are much higher than on the dayside [1][4]. The sources reviewed do not state thermal, radiation, lunar-night or mechanical environmental tolerances for any of the examples.
article.limitations: A small number of campaigns can sample only a limited range of geometries, times and plasma conditions. The Chandrayaan-2 DFRS experiments were conducted on four occasions, with twelve occultation experiments in total [1]. Results depend on modelling and interpretation. The ISRO wake-region ion composition is a numerical model result [2], and the Apollo-era ionospheric evidence is described as model-dependent [8]. The TEC measurements carry an uncertainty of 0.15 TECU [1]. The retrieval assumptions used in Earth GNSS radio occultation, including near spherical symmetry, may not transfer directly to the Moon [5]. Finally, the flown Chandrayaan-2 configuration uses an Earth ground station; an instrument that relies on a different receiver geometry would have different limitations.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Radio occultation of the lunar ionosphere is an orbital measurement. For Chandrayaan-2, the DFRS is an experiment on the orbiter, which was launched by ISRO on 22 July 2019 [2]. The sources reviewed do not describe Earth integration, cruise, lunar orbit insertion, commissioning or the spacecraft pointing and thermal interfaces used by the DFRS, so these items are not assessed. The RIPLIO concept requires at least two CubeSats in lunar orbit, with one transmitting and one receiving to form a crosslink [4]. A surface-mounted occultation receiver is not the configuration described in the flown or proposed examples, and rover, mobile and sample-return configurations are not applicable to the examples reviewed.
transportation_process: Orbiter payload (Chandrayaan-2 DFRS): the DFRS is an experiment on the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which ISRO launched on 22 July 2019 [2]. Earth integration and launch configuration are not described in the sources reviewed.
Cruise and lunar orbit insertion: not described in the sources reviewed for the DFRS; not assessed.
Commissioning and pointing, thermal and data interfaces: not described in the sources reviewed; not assessed.
Operations (DFRS): campaign-mode occultation experiments, twelve in total on four occasions, using the Byalalu ground station [1].

RIPLIO concept: at least two CubeSats in lunar orbit, with one VHF transmitter and one broadband receiver forming a crosslink [4]. Launch, release, orbit insertion and relative-geometry maintenance are not described in the sources reviewed.
Surface and other configurations: a surface-only occultation instrument is not described in the examples reviewed. Compatibility with any named lander, rover or spacecraft is not asserted.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For the flown Chandrayaan-2 DFRS, the radio-science experiment operates from the orbiter using the orbiter's coherent S-band and X-band signals [1][2]. No deployment mechanism is described in the sources reviewed. The proposed RIPLIO concept would place two CubeSats in lunar orbit, but the deployment method is not described [4].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 15 command module signal test and the Apollo 15 and 16 subsatellites are historical examples of radio links used to probe the lunar environment [6][7]. The Chandrayaan-2 DFRS is the flown dual-frequency example [1].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. Compatibility with a specific lunar spacecraft requires verified interface evidence, which was not obtained in this run.

article.historical_significance: Radio links between spacecraft and Earth have been used to probe the lunar environment since the Apollo era. The 1971 Apollo 15 test, in which the command module's signals were received after it passed behind the lunar limb, is a historical example of this approach [6]. Apollo-era interpretations of the lunar ionosphere remain uncertain and model-dependent [8]. The Chandrayaan-2 DFRS is a flown, dedicated dual-frequency radio science experiment that has reported wake-region electron content and plasma density [1][3]. The RIPLIO concept, proposed in 2023, illustrates how a CubeSat pair could be used to map the lunar ionosphere in future missions [4].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The payload name describes a measurement technique rather than a single instrument, so the figures above describe specific experiments and concepts, not a generic radio occultation instrument. Only one of the three examples has flown, and its published values come from ISRO web pages and a journal reference. The full text of the Tripathi et al. journal article was not accessed in this run, so values are as reported by the ISRO summary [1][2][3]. The mass, power and dimensions of the Chandrayaan-2 DFRS hardware are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. The RIPLIO values are simulation outputs and concept requirements, not measurements [4][9]. Several sources were available only as search-result summaries because the publisher page or PDF returned an access error during this run. These include the Watson et al. article [4], the 1971 Nature letter [6], the ROLSS/arXiv paper [8], the NASA Apollo 16 subsatellite page [7], the CAP 2025 abstract [9] and the Current Science article [10].

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values, and all other URL fields in this file, have query strings and fragments removed. No image objects are included in this version because no direct image asset URL was verified from an official page within the research budget. Section-level image arrays are present and empty.

data_quality_notes: No images were verified or included. The Markdown article contains no images, and the image arrays are empty.
The Chandrayaan-2 DFRS mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed (ISRO DFRS pages). No values are estimated.
The Tripathi et al. MNRAS Letters article (DOI 10.1093/mnrasl/slac058) was cited via the ISRO summary; the full text was not accessed. Publication year is not confirmed in the sources reviewed.

The Watson et al. (Radio Science 2023, DOI 10.1029/2023RS007666) full text returned HTTP 403 and was not accessed. Its details (two CubeSats, VHF transmitter at multiple frequencies, broadband receiver, simulation results) come from a search-result summary; the specific frequencies and sensitivities are not verified.
The Current Science oscillator stability (about 10^-11) is from a search-result summary; the article was not fetched (DNS error on i-scholar.in). Treat as unverified.
The 1971 Nature letter on Apollo 15 CSM signals was not read (redirect to an authentication page). The statement is from a search-result summary.
The ROLSS/arXiv paper PDF returned binary content and was not read as text. The Bauer (1996) interpretation and the ALSEP photoelectron-layer statement are from a search-result summary.
The 2025 CAP Congress abstract (Radaelli et al.) is cited from a search-result summary; its statement about lower HF frequencies and few-MHz spacings is unverified.
The NASA Apollo 16 subsatellite page is cited from a search-result summary; the S-band transponder statement is unverified against the page itself.
The Watson et al. paper describes VHF signals. The search-result summary of a 2025 abstract mentions HF frequencies; these are not reconciled.

The JPL GENESIS background page was read and supports the general GNSS radio occultation description used in the Operating Principle section. Its altitude ranges (ionosphere about 60-1,000 km; neutral atmosphere about 0-50 km) apply to Earth and are not used as lunar values.
No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted; transportation compatibility was not verified.

Search and fetch budget: 6 WebSearch calls were used. WebFetch calls were made to the ISRO pages, JPL GENESIS page and several publisher and PDF URLs; several returned access errors (HTTP 403 and 405, DNS failure) or binary PDF content. No MCP tools were called.
